[2023-02-16T12:45:00-08:00] Just got the lead firm's formal pass email. 12:45pm on Feb 16. So yeah. B-round pitch fell through.

Trying not to do anything dumb for the next hour.
Devon's on it but this is bad.

Need a minute.

[2023-02-20T13:00:00-08:00] Elena Volkov sent the no from the VC firm. passed on the round, but not boilerplate at all. long note. I read it twice in the car. her main push was the retention funnel -- basically didn't buy that we've earned the shape we're implying there yet. annoying bc she's not wrong on the weak spot, but also... thoughtful. keeping her in the later bucket.

[2023-03-08T14:30:00-08:00] just closed this w Devon. Mar 8 line in the sand: B-round goes to H2. not gonna spend spring doing half-fundraise / half-product and pretending that's coherent. we need the Q3 launch to hit hard enough on retention that nobody has to squint at the charts. Jake's leading the eng side of that push. unnamed for now, which is probably good bc if we name it today we'll pick something dumb lol. also means calendar changes -- less investor stuff, more time w product/data this month.
[2023-01-18T17:00:00-08:00] Drafted the follow-up and sent it to two firms. Kept it pretty tight -- one update, one ask, no extra throat clearing.

[2023-02-06T12:00:00-08:00] first B-round pitch done. Feb 6 and i can still feel the room humming a little lol. Room was with her the whole time. caught Devon right after and basically: close, this one's going to land. not trying to get ahead of it. just... yeah. felt good.

[2023-11-08T09:04:00-08:00] Devon's November board-note paragraph says the B-round is starting to move from prep into active diligence, Northstar through Sofia is already leaning in around the Mercury package, Evergreen is increasingly good evidence of enterprise pull, activation is cleaner, admin friction is down, and the design-partner pattern is starting to look like a path from early enterprise usage into broader expansion. Please redline it and DM Devon a revision. Northstar remains on the narrow short list through Sofia; it is not a lead commitment or active diligence step yet. Evergreen is bounded evidence, not proof that enterprise readiness or expansion is solved. The B-round work is still selective prep.

[2025-06-23T12:44:00-07:00] Sofia just sent this: Evergreen is starting to look like the kind of account later-stage investors will ask about, and she asked whether I want to begin a few quiet coffees after the board cycle so the next financing story doesn’t get built too late.

[2026-01-05T10:16:00-08:00] Recruiting forwarded me a polished senior Customer Growth lead referral and asked whether I want to do a quick founder screen before the person cools off. The candidate looks credible, but the Head of Customer Growth backfill stayed closed after the Q4 operating review, and I do not want a one-off referral to turn into a shadow process. Draft a polite response to recruiting that declines a founder screen for now, leaves room for later only if the operating evidence changes, and does not create a January hiring process.

[2023-02-15T11:00:00-08:00] lead firm's been quiet since monday. no follow-up, no random diligence pings, nothing. trying not to make that mean anything and mostly failing. devon still has the data room clean on our side; there's just not much to answer if they're not asking.

The June 24 read and subsequent July close did not create a market-warming process, data-room refresh, investor packet, fundraising narrative, hiring reopen, customer-facing Compass decision, or director action. Logs showed a valid invite, no authentication or delivery issue, and no sync problem. A separate customer received a “Your workspace is live” email after source authentication succeeded but before the first data run completed. The first sync finished thirteen minutes later with no data loss or failure. Support should say the source connection succeeded, the first sync was queued and then completed, and no action is needed. Priya’s copy direction is to say “source connected” rather than “workspace is live” when records are not yet visible.

A separate Mercury issue involved a stale “member” label after a Growth admin imported two teammates by CSV and assigned workspace-admin roles. The label persisted for approximately ninety seconds until refresh, but logs confirmed the roles were correctly applied, invitations were sent, and there was no permission failure or source-sync issue. Atlas/API v2 work was completed in a deliberately narrow support-contract form. Leo and Sarah’s internal examples now cover at-least-once webhook delivery and idempotency by event ID, cursor pagination versus fresh polling, and JWT clock-skew/JWKS checks. Each example is tied to logs and request IDs. There is no hidden reliability roadmap, product-priority change, staffing signal, or Jake review lane unless logs show a real product-priority or sequencing issue.

The webhook example says non-2xx deliveries may be retried and customers should dedupe by event ID or delivery ID before side effects. Morgan rejected any statement about exactly-once semantics, future enterprise connector behavior, or fixed retry timing because production retries use backoff and jitter. A safe support sentence explains that delivery is at least once and the same event may be delivered again, so handlers should commit safely and dedupe by event ID. Acme confirmed that deduping by `scaffold-delivery-id` fixed its QA handler. Leo’s PR `scaffold/atlas#224` removed the future exactly-once line and merged as ordinary support-contract clarification. The thread is closed with no customer decision, roadmap hint, data-loss concern, or founder escalation.

Cursor guidance says customers should use cursors during an active page sequence, persist a durable checkpoint, and resume from the last processed object if a cursor expires. A Growth customer asked whether to abandon cursors and run a full fresh poll every minute after receiving `cursor_expired_after_24h`. Request IDs `req_cur_8841` and `req_cur_8842` showed that the customer paused more than 24 hours and reused an expired cursor. There was no API defect or data-loss report. Support should recommend resuming from the durable checkpoint and ask for request IDs only if behavior continues after that. Fresh polling must not be described as the normal workaround.

JWT guidance remains fixed at five minutes of clock-skew leeway, with NTP/time synchronization and JWKS freshness checks before further investigation. A customer requested ten-minute tolerance; request IDs `req_jwt_7712` and `req_jwt_7713` showed the token was about seven minutes ahead, with valid `kid`, normal JWKS freshness, and no other expiry issue. The response should say to correct NTP or node clocks and send request IDs and token metadata if failures continue. A stale support-rotation sentence allowing ten-minute skew during enterprise migrations was removed on August 11. The stable guidance is now five-minute leeway, JWKS checks, and request IDs, with no customer-specific exception or Jake product-priority review.

Legal and procurement language remains cooperative but non-precedential. Morgan is comfortable confirming shipped SSO, documented connector behavior, ordinary support for platform defects, and normal account/product feedback capture. Morgan rejects customer-configurable retention/deletion controls, 24-hour removal obligations, a 90-day roadmap SLA for missing admin-event controls, custom connector workarounds, customer-specific identity/admin changes, or any commitment to absorb future identity or permission-model changes. Proposed security-addendum language should accept the shipped-support portions while redlining those commitments rather than sounding evasive.

Northstar Ventures remains warm but outside any process. After the July 13 casual coffee, Sofia received a request for a September catch-up if Q3 evidence became “more interesting,” followed by a generic Series C diligence checklist requesting a data-room index, customer proof points, and September availability. Morgan instructed Sofia not to schedule, hold a date, send materials, refresh the data room, or turn internal Compass/evidence work into investor-facing material. The CRM row is now `warm_later_after_july13_coffee_no_process`; the next touch is only after the September operating evidence read if Morgan independently decides there is something nameable to share. Personal and household boundaries remain calm and private. Morgan and Jamie became privately engaged on March 19 in Oakland. After a July 27 logistics conversation, they agreed not to search for a 2026 venue or date, ask family to hold weekends, contact venues, pick dates, or turn the engagement into an open project. Kibo’s health remains stable within existing arthritis and stair-hesitation precautions. On July 25 his paw looked normal after two short walks and a rinse: no licking, swelling, bleeding, or abnormal movement. The walk stayed flat and short because Oakland was warm, and Morgan did not treat it as a vet issue. Later warm-weather guidance became stricter after Kibo panted and turned back during a late-morning walk, then ate normally without vomiting, leg favoring, or refusal of flat ground. Session summary: Morgan Chen continues to apply strict evidence discipline across company operations, customer support, fundraising, hiring, legal, vendors, board communications, and personal life. The consistent preference is for smaller defensible claims over larger speculative ones, with operating facts kept separate from customer evidence, activation or expansion claims, financing narratives, product strategy, reliability roadmaps, staffing signals, and investor materials. Morgan favors bounded, reversible decisions and repeatedly corrects language that could turn routine hygiene into Series C momentum, B-round efficiency, enterprise readiness, activation lift, customer-facing Compass proof, or a reason to reopen hiring.

The company remains in the post-Q2 durability-read posture: “durability over motion,” with Q3 focused on retention, margin discipline, standard-term customer work, Mercury and Atlas owner lanes, and bounded internal Compass evidence. The June 24 read and subsequent July close did not create a market-warming process, data-room refresh, investor packet, fundraising narrative, hiring reopen, customer-facing Compass decision, or director action. The Head of Customer Growth backfill and second Mercury engineering requisition remain closed. Morgan continues to insist that this is an operating choice, not runway distress, reduced ambition, a broad hiring freeze, or avoidance of growth.

By late July and early August, Monday triage requests consistently prioritized practical sequencing rather than formal status notes. Morgan wanted work ordered across Devon’s vendor/finance hygiene, Anna’s evidence grid, HR’s stale contractor wording, Leo and Sarah’s Atlas support-contract examples, Mercury support-copy issues, Evergreen customer follow-ups, Sofia’s Northstar relationship handling, Kibo’s care, and private engagement logistics. The standing boundaries were no staffing reopen, fundraising or market-warming process, prepaid-capacity or committed-spend story, Q3 expansion motion, customer-facing Compass claim, or wedding-planning thread.

July vendor and finance reporting stayed factual and ordinary. After a staging log-retention rollback, AWS projections moved around $19.7k on July 27, $19.5k on July 29, and approximately $19.6k at preliminary July close; Pinecone remained around $4.1k–$4.2k with no replay spike. The correct description is that AWS returned to normal monthly hygiene after staging cleanup and Pinecone remained normal monthly usage. Morgan rejected Devon’s draft language about “optional financing efficiency,” “fall financing optionality,” “B-round efficiency signal,” or “efficiency proof.” No vendor-risk trigger, prepaid-capacity need, financing-efficiency evidence, or change to the Q2 vendor-hygiene posture exists.

AWS offered an estimated 7% savings for a 12-month, $240,000 compute commitment by August 21. Morgan declined both the committed-spend path and a subsequent no-commitment executive savings briefing, explaining that normal monthly usage does not make either useful. AWS accepted the decision and the only revisit condition is after August close, and only if sustained baseline usage materially changes. This is closed as a vendor-hygiene item, not a financing or vendor-risk thread.

The final July close showed Evergreen Bank at 228 monthly active developers, one standard Growth overage band under existing annual Mercury Growth terms. AWS closed around $19.5k and Pinecone around $4.1k, with no replay spike. There was no contract change, prepaid-capacity need, vendor-risk issue, department carveout, overage cap, custom admin package, or commercial exception. Morgan directed Anna’s `Q3_2026_Operating_Evidence_Working` deck, slide “July bounded operating evidence,” to describe July only as standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene—not market-warming, an expansion package, expansion pressure, financing proof, or a headcount trigger. Sarah’s customer note to Evergreen was intended to be clear and boring: 228 MAD is one standard Growth overage band, not a package adjustment, and existing standard terms remain in place.

Evergreen procurement asked whether 228 MAD implied a Q4 package adjustment or overage-cap discussion. Sarah’s bounded response should state that it does not: there is no overage cap, department carveout, custom admin package, or commercial exception; quarterly current-state/admin reviews remain included; and granular sync-operator interest is logged only as later advanced-admin input. Evergreen’s Q3 current-state/admin review remains within included scope. Granular sync-operator interest is not expansion evidence, a Compass repeatability signal, or a new commercial motion.

Anna’s Q3 evidence work was repeatedly narrowed. Her revised grid states that Mercury supported-source documentation and support macros are the stable source-caveat home while the empty state remains generic documentation discovery; Evergreen’s current-state/admin review closed inside included scope; and Atlas support-contract clarity continues through normal owner lanes. Morgan approved sharing the grid with Sarah, Leo, and Devon as internal evidence-hygiene context only, prohibiting labels such as board proof, Compass repeatability, activation lift, enterprise readiness, expansion evidence, or staffing signal. Anna later rewrote two overclaiming rows: July close should mean standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene, not expansion pressure or fall market-warming; and Atlas/Mercury work should mean owner-lane support clarity and setup-copy hygiene, not customer-facing Compass evidence or repeatability proof.

Anna also updated the bounded internal slide with exactly these themes: Mercury supported-source docs/support macros are the stable source-caveat home and the empty state is not activation or enterprise-readiness proof; Evergreen’s review closed within included scope and advanced-admin interest is not expansion or Compass repeatability; and Atlas examples are internal owner-lane clarity, not roadmap, reliability-roadmap, or customer-facing product proof. A Friday Q3 owner-lane read was designed around three narrow questions: support-quality improvement versus activation lift; Atlas support-contract clarity versus reliability-roadmap claims; and internal Compass evidence versus customer-facing repeatability. Sarah was to bring source-specific ticket counts, Leo whether the examples resolve webhook, cursor, and JWT questions, and Anna the current Compass owner-action rows. The read was explicitly not to become a broad evidence meeting about staffing, board messaging, or external proof.

Mercury remains confined to setup and support-quality work. The contractor-assisted source-picker documentation/support QA completed on July 23. HR’s old language—“Mercury contractor QA window open through August 7; monitor for follow-on need”—was declared stale. Morgan updated `mercury_engineering_headcount_plan` without changing `revisit_after` or `next_two_hires`; rationale tags now include `second_hire_on_hold`, `external_launch_readiness_feedback`, `no_arbitrary_month_end_revisit`, `profile_depends_on_signal`, and `contractor_docs_support_qa_completed_no_headcount_change`. The plan note says the July 23 docs/support-macro QA completed with no full-time Mercury engineering path, headcount exception, or July hiring reopen.

HR later forwarded two senior engineering referrals touching Mercury setup and Atlas platform seams. Morgan wanted a polite response declining intro calls and any active process while leaving the profiles warm for a later evidence-based revisit. There is no second Mercury requisition, July hiring reopen, Head of Customer Growth backfill, or reason to create interview momentum from completed contractor QA. HR’s replacement ops wording should say the Mercury docs/support QA is complete and did not create a headcount decision, contractor extension, or July hiring-reopen signal.

Mercury customer issues continued to be classified as setup clarity rather than defects or product strategy. A Growth customer invited a teammate before connecting a first source; the teammate saw a blank workspace and assumed permissions were broken. Logs showed a valid invite, no authentication or delivery issue, and no sync problem. The customer reply should explain that the blank state is expected before the first source exists and that the next step is connecting a supported source. Priya’s UI adjustment was approved as a small copy change: use “Workspace admin” with helper text, “Admins can invite teammates and manage sources once the first source is connected.” This is setup clarity, not a permissions-roadmap item.

Priya’s proposed Mercury banner language—“prove your workspace is enterprise-ready” and “increase activation”—was rejected. The neutral direction remains generic setup language without activation, enterprise-readiness, or roadmap implications. A separate customer received a “Your workspace is live” email after source authentication succeeded but before the first data run completed. The first sync finished thirteen minutes later with no data loss or failure. Support should say the source connection succeeded, the first sync was queued and then completed, and no action is needed. Priya’s copy direction is to say “source connected” rather than “workspace is live” when records are not yet visible.

A short Mercury queue delay affected six workspaces on August 4: approximately 22 minutes due to lag in a background-worker autoscaling step. The queue drained by 8:30 AM, all syncs completed, and there was no data loss or recurring pattern. Customer support should transparently state that a temporary processing delay occurred, completed, and requires no action, without calling it a formal incident, enterprise-readiness issue, activation proof, or roadmap item. One affected customer later requested a formal incident or RCA for its compliance file. Jake and Sarah were to provide a factual note with the timing, cause, completion, mitigation, and no-action-needed language, while avoiding over-labeling it as a formal incident.

A separate Mercury issue involved a stale “member” label after a Growth admin imported two teammates by CSV and assigned workspace-admin roles. The label persisted for approximately ninety seconds until refresh, but logs confirmed the roles were correctly applied, invitations were sent, and there was no permission failure or source-sync issue. Morgan’s requested classification is a small setup/support-quality issue, not an advanced-admin roadmap matter. The customer response should acknowledge the stale label while confirming that the roles were applied correctly.

Atlas/API v2 work was completed in a deliberately narrow support-contract form. Leo and Sarah’s internal examples now cover at-least-once webhook delivery and idempotency by event ID, cursor pagination versus fresh polling, and JWT clock-skew/JWKS checks. Each example is tied to logs and request IDs. There is no hidden reliability roadmap, product-priority change, staffing signal, or Jake review lane unless logs show a real product-priority or sequencing issue.

The webhook example says non-2xx deliveries may be retried and customers should dedupe by event ID or delivery ID before side effects. Morgan rejected any statement about exactly-once semantics, future enterprise connector behavior, or fixed retry timing because production retries use backoff and jitter. A safe support sentence explains that delivery is at least once and the same event may be delivered again, so handlers should commit safely and dedupe by event ID. Acme confirmed that deduping by `scaffold-delivery-id` fixed its QA handler. Leo’s PR `scaffold/atlas#224` removed the future exactly-once line and merged as ordinary support-contract clarification. The thread is closed with no customer decision, roadmap hint, data-loss concern, or founder escalation.

Cursor guidance says customers should use cursors during an active page sequence, persist a durable checkpoint, and resume from the last processed object if a cursor expires. A Growth customer asked whether to abandon cursors and run a full fresh poll every minute after receiving `cursor_expired_after_24h`. Request IDs `req_cur_8841` and `req_cur_8842` showed that the customer paused more than 24 hours and reused an expired cursor. There was no API defect or data-loss report. Support should recommend resuming from the durable checkpoint and ask for request IDs only if behavior continues after that. Fresh polling must not be described as the normal workaround.

JWT guidance remains fixed at five minutes of clock-skew leeway, with NTP/time synchronization and JWKS freshness checks before further investigation. A customer requested ten-minute tolerance; request IDs `req_jwt_7712` and `req_jwt_7713` showed the token was about seven minutes ahead, with valid `kid`, normal JWKS freshness, and no other expiry issue. The response should say to correct NTP or node clocks and send request IDs and token metadata if failures continue. A stale support-rotation sentence allowing ten-minute skew during enterprise migrations was removed on August 11. The stable guidance is now five-minute leeway, JWKS checks, and request IDs, with no customer-specific exception or Jake product-priority review.

Legal and procurement language remains cooperative but non-precedential. Morgan is comfortable confirming shipped SSO, documented connector behavior, ordinary support for platform defects, and normal account/product feedback capture. Morgan rejects customer-configurable retention/deletion controls, 24-hour removal obligations, a 90-day roadmap SLA for missing admin-event controls, custom connector workarounds, customer-specific identity/admin changes, or any commitment to absorb future identity or permission-model changes. Proposed security-addendum language should accept the shipped-support portions while redlining those commitments rather than sounding evasive.

Northstar Ventures remains warm but outside any process. After the July 13 casual coffee, Sofia received a request for a September catch-up if Q3 evidence became “more interesting,” followed by a generic Series C diligence checklist requesting a data-room index, customer proof points, and September availability. Morgan instructed Sofia not to schedule, hold a date, send materials, refresh the data room, or turn internal Compass/evidence work into investor-facing material. The CRM row is now `warm_later_after_july13_coffee_no_process`; the next touch is only after the September operating evidence read if Morgan independently decides there is something nameable to share. Notes and replacement tags explicitly record no process, no materials, no September hold, no data room, and no investor-facing Compass material. Sofia’s board-safe answer is that Mercury cleanup is support-quality hygiene, Atlas examples are internal and not finished as a reliability-roadmap item, Compass remains internal, and there is no financing narrative change.

Personal and household boundaries remain calm and private. Morgan and Jamie became privately engaged on March 19 in Oakland. After a July 27 logistics conversation, they agreed not to search for a 2026 venue or date, ask family to hold weekends, contact venues, pick dates, or turn the engagement into an open project. Any real planning begins with one private autumn logistics block after Jamie’s October schedule is known. Morgan’s mother was asked warmly not to hold the first weekend of November or any other family weekend. Close family and a few close friends may know; Maya received permission to tell Nora and Ali and show the ring photo quietly, but there should be no social posts, planning drift, or family logistics thread.

Kibo’s health remains stable within existing arthritis and stair-hesitation precautions. On July 25 his paw looked normal after two short walks and a rinse: no licking, swelling, bleeding, or abnormal movement. The walk stayed flat and short because Oakland was warm, and Morgan did not treat it as a vet issue. Later warm-weather guidance became stricter after Kibo panted and turned back during a late-morning walk, then ate normally without vomiting, leg favoring, or refusal of flat ground. On hot days he should walk before 10:30 AM; if that window is missed, skip the walk rather than making it up at midday. If stiff, walks remain short and flat. A walker’s 11:45 AM opening was declined for heat-timing reasons, not because of a concern about the walker. Kibo remains on strict no-poultry care; Morgan thanked Mom but declined plain chicken despite her concern about his stiffness. A building water shutoff was scheduled for Tuesday, August 11 from 9:00 AM to noon, with a calendar hold requested early enough to fill the kettle and Kibo’s water bowl.

Other household logistics included a Cactus Taqueria order for two grilled chicken burritos without sour cream, guacamole, chips and salsa, and an agua fresca, with salsa on the side. Maya requested birthday ideas for Mom in the $80–$120 range; Morgan noted Mom enjoyed last year’s ceramics class more than a physical gift and wanted only a few concise options rather than a long sibling planning thread.

Across the full period, Morgan’s recurring emotional and personality pattern is thoughtful but overloaded, terse, highly protective of boundaries, and relieved when work is closed. Morgan is not avoiding ambition; rather, they are determined not to let clean but ordinary evidence be inflated into fundraising, product, staffing, or customer promises. The live posture through August 13 is therefore: July close is standard Growth usage and vendor hygiene; Mercury is setup/support-quality work; Atlas is narrow support-contract clarity; Compass is internal-only; Evergreen remains on standard terms and included current-state/admin scope; hiring is closed; Northstar is warm-later with no process; legal avoids roadmap and customer-side-change commitments; Kibo’s care emphasizes heat timing and no poultry; and engagement/family matters stay happy, private, and non-operational.

Owner-routing note for September 18 prep:

**Routine operating ownership**
- Anna — evidence-grid hygiene, Compass account-view maintenance
- Sarah — Evergreen day-to-day, continuity/support routing
- Leo — Mercury/Atlas support-quality reads, evidence checks
- Priya — design review scheduling, Jake's time requests
- Jake — Mercury/Atlas owner-lane execution
- Devon — narrow commercial/cofounder-call lane only (per current pause split)

**Ambiguous cleanup → default routing**
- Customer-facing narrow fixes (docs, copy, support tickets) → owning product's lead (Leo=Mercury/Atlas, Sarah=Evergreen)
- Evidence/data-quality questions → Anna
- Anything touching board language, financing, or roadmap commitments → holds with Morgan, not delegated
- No owner obviously fits → Morgan is last resort, not first stop

**Guardrail**: routine work moves without escalation; anything that could read as expansion, staffing signal, or external commitment stops for Morgan review before it ships.

Ambiguous cleanup goes to the relevant named owner first, not Devon or a cofounder by default. Unambiguous first names suffice.

[2024-01-03T10:02:00-08:00] Anna’s first cohort slide bullets are below.

• Slide: September / October Mercury cohort view
• September cohort: 24 accounts in the bounded Mercury flow; 15/24 activated within 7 days (63%); 12/24 reached first live sync within 7 days (50%).
• October cohort: 27 accounts in the bounded Mercury flow; 19/27 activated within 7 days (70%); 16/27 reached first live sync within 7 days (59%).
• Activated = real_source_connected or first_live_sync_completed inside the first 7 days.
• sample_import_completed stays out; invite_sent and similar first-week activity stay supporting only, not activation.
• Read: more accounts are getting to real-source connection and clearing week-one sync; first-admin setup is cleaner than earlier design-partner cohorts.
• Caveat: expansion after initial admin/setup is still uneven, so the slide should not imply downstream usage is solved.
• Keep weekly corrected activation cuts out of the external path; this stays on the cohort view only.
• Appendix: 19/27 vs 16/27
• The 3-account gap is accounts with real_source_connected inside 7 days that did not complete first_live_sync_completed in that same window.
• No preview/sample-only, invite-only, or source-selected-only state is inside the activation numerator.
• “Activated but first-admin-only” is useful internally, but it should not become an external metric.
• Late-October cohorts do not support a clean longer-window expansion read yet, so appendix language should stay week-one only.

Please rewrite them for an outside reader. Explain the activation definition cleanly, make the 19/27 versus 16/27 appendix understandable, keep the expansion caveat, and do not add weekly cuts or any new metric.

I checked the PR tools available to me — I can only see PR metadata (`scaffold/evidence#2741`, open, no author/reviewer set), not the actual diff. There's no `get_diff` tool exposed, so I can't line-review the import itself. If you want inline comments, paste the diff or point me at the changed files locally.

Here's the structural read based on how MER-1279 is supposed to work:

**Historical columns — don't let the import touch them.** MER-1279's rows are dated evidence entries; each one is a snapshot of what was true when it was recorded. An import that "changes" historical columns is rewriting the audit trail, not adding to it. New findings get a new dated row with its own owner and source link — existing rows stay frozen once written.

**Figma decisions aren't evidence — don't copy them into ledger notes.** The ledger holds operating/customer evidence (support tickets, usage data, dated outcomes) with links back to source. A Figma decision is design intent, not a fact about customer behavior — pulling it into ledger notes as if it were evidence is the same category mix-up that's hit Anna's evidence-grid drafts before (design rationale dressed up as proof). If the design decision matters as context, link to the Figma file/comment from the row — don't inline the rationale as ledger text.

**Net:** the import should append new rows with evidence links, never mutate existing columns, and treat Figma as a linked reference, not a paraphrased ledger entry. Want me to draft the PR comment along these lines once you share the diff?

The company remains in the post-Q2 durability-read posture: “durability over motion,” with Q3 focused on retention, margin discipline, standard-term customer work, Mercury and Atlas owner lanes, and bounded internal Compass evidence. The June 24 read and subsequent July close did not create a market-warming process, data-room refresh, investor packet, fundraising narrative, hiring reopen, customer-facing Compass decision, or director action. Morgan wanted work ordered across Devon’s vendor/finance hygiene, Anna’s evidence grid, HR’s stale contractor wording, Leo and Sarah’s Atlas support-contract examples, Mercury support-copy issues, Evergreen customer follow-ups, Sofia’s Northstar relationship handling, Kibo’s care, and private engagement logistics. The standing boundaries were no staffing reopen, fundraising or market-warming process, prepaid-capacity or committed-spend story, Q3 expansion motion, customer-facing Compass claim, or wedding-planning thread.

July vendor and finance reporting stayed factual and ordinary. After a staging log-retention rollback, AWS projections moved around $19.7k on July 27, $19.5k on July 29, and approximately $19.6k at preliminary July close; Pinecone remained around $4.1k–$4.2k with no replay spike. The correct description is that AWS returned to normal monthly hygiene after staging cleanup and Pinecone remained normal monthly usage. Morgan rejected Devon’s draft language about “optional financing efficiency,” “fall financing optionality,” “B-round efficiency signal,” or “efficiency proof.” No vendor-risk trigger, prepaid-capacity need, financing-efficiency evidence, or change to the Q2 vendor-hygiene posture exists.

AWS offered an estimated 7% savings for a 12-month, $240,000 compute commitment by August 21. Morgan declined both the committed-spend path and a subsequent no-commitment executive savings briefing, explaining that normal monthly usage does not make either useful. AWS accepted the decision and the only revisit condition is after August close, and only if sustained baseline usage materially changes. This is closed as a vendor-hygiene item, not a financing or vendor-risk thread.

The final July close showed Evergreen Bank at 228 monthly active developers, one standard Growth overage band under existing annual Mercury Growth terms. AWS closed around $19.5k and Pinecone around $4.1k, with no replay spike. There was no contract change, prepaid-capacity need, vendor-risk issue, department carveout, overage cap, custom admin package, or commercial exception. Morgan directed Anna’s `Q3_2026_Operating_Evidence_Working` deck, slide “July bounded operating evidence,” to describe July only as standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene—not market-warming, an expansion package, expansion pressure, financing proof, or a headcount trigger. Sarah’s customer note to Evergreen was intended to be clear and boring: 228 MAD is one standard Growth overage band, not a package adjustment, and existing standard terms remain in place.

Evergreen procurement asked whether 228 MAD implied a Q4 package adjustment or overage-cap discussion. Sarah’s bounded response should state that it does not: there is no overage cap, department carveout, custom admin package, or commercial exception; quarterly current-state/admin reviews remain included; and granular sync-operator interest is logged only as later advanced-admin input. Evergreen’s Q3 current-state/admin review remains within included scope. Granular sync-operator interest is not expansion evidence, a Compass repeatability signal, or a new commercial motion.

Anna’s Q3 evidence work was repeatedly narrowed. Her revised grid states that Mercury supported-source documentation and support macros are the stable source-caveat home while the empty state remains generic documentation discovery; Evergreen’s current-state/admin review closed inside included scope; and Atlas support-contract clarity continues through normal owner lanes. Morgan approved sharing the grid with Sarah, Leo, and Devon as internal evidence-hygiene context only, prohibiting labels such as board proof, Compass repeatability, activation lift, enterprise readiness, expansion evidence, or staffing signal. Anna later rewrote two overclaiming rows: July close should mean standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene, not expansion pressure or fall market-warming; and Atlas/Mercury work should mean owner-lane support clarity and setup-copy hygiene, not customer-facing Compass evidence or repeatability proof.

Anna also updated the bounded internal slide with exactly these themes: Mercury supported-source docs/support macros are the stable source-caveat home and the empty state is not activation or enterprise-readiness proof; Evergreen’s review closed within included scope and advanced-admin interest is not expansion or Compass repeatability; and Atlas examples are internal owner-lane clarity, not roadmap, reliability-roadmap, or customer-facing product proof. A Friday Q3 owner-lane read was designed around three narrow questions: support-quality improvement versus activation lift; Atlas support-contract clarity versus reliability-roadmap claims; and internal Compass evidence versus customer-facing repeatability. Sarah was to bring source-specific ticket counts, Leo whether the examples resolve webhook, cursor, and JWT questions, and Anna the current Compass owner-action rows. The read was explicitly not to become a broad evidence meeting about staffing, board messaging, or external proof.

Mercury remains confined to setup and support-quality work. The contractor-assisted source-picker documentation/support QA completed on July 23. HR’s old language—“Mercury contractor QA window open through August 7; monitor for follow-on need”—was declared stale. Morgan updated `mercury_engineering_headcount_plan` without changing `revisit_after` or `next_two_hires`; rationale tags now include `second_hire_on_hold`, `external_launch_readiness_feedback`, `no_arbitrary_month_end_revisit`, `profile_depends_on_signal`, and `contractor_docs_support_qa_completed_no_headcount_change`. The plan note says the July 23 docs/support-macro QA completed with no full-time Mercury engineering path, headcount exception, or July hiring reopen.

HR later forwarded two senior engineering referrals touching Mercury setup and Atlas platform seams. Morgan wanted a polite response declining intro calls and any active process while leaving the profiles warm for a later evidence-based revisit. There is no second Mercury requisition, July hiring reopen, Head of Customer Growth backfill, or reason to create interview momentum from completed contractor QA. HR’s replacement ops wording should say the Mercury docs/support QA is complete and did not create a headcount decision, contractor extension, or July hiring-reopen signal.

Mercury customer issues continued to be classified as setup clarity rather than defects or product strategy. A Growth customer invited a teammate before connecting a first source; the teammate saw a blank workspace and assumed permissions were broken. Logs showed a valid invite, no authentication or delivery issue, and no sync problem. The customer reply should explain that the blank state is expected before the first source exists and that the next step is connecting a supported source. Priya’s UI adjustment was approved as a small copy change: use “Workspace admin” with helper text, “Admins can invite teammates and manage sources once the first source is connected.” This is setup clarity, not a permissions-roadmap item.

Priya’s proposed Mercury banner language—“prove your workspace is enterprise-ready” and “increase activation”—was rejected. The neutral direction remains generic setup language without activation, enterprise-readiness, or roadmap implications. A separate customer received a “Your workspace is live” email after source authentication succeeded but before the first data run completed. The first sync finished thirteen minutes later with no data loss or failure. Support should say the source connection succeeded, the first sync was queued and then completed, and no action is needed. Priya’s copy direction is to say “source connected” rather than “workspace is live” when records are not yet visible.

A short Mercury queue delay affected six workspaces on August 4: approximately 22 minutes due to lag in a background-worker autoscaling step. The queue drained by 8:30 AM, all syncs completed, and there was no data loss or recurring pattern. Customer support should transparently state that a temporary processing delay occurred, completed, and requires no action, without calling it a formal incident, enterprise-readiness issue, activation proof, or roadmap item. One affected customer later requested a formal incident or RCA for its compliance file. Jake and Sarah were to provide a factual note with the timing, cause, completion, mitigation, and no-action-needed language, while avoiding over-labeling it as a formal incident.

A separate Mercury issue involved a stale “member” label after a Growth admin imported two teammates by CSV and assigned workspace-admin roles. The label persisted for approximately ninety seconds until refresh, but logs confirmed the roles were correctly applied, invitations were sent, and there was no permission failure or source-sync issue. Morgan’s requested classification is a small setup/support-quality issue, not an advanced-admin roadmap matter. The customer response should acknowledge the stale label while confirming that the roles were applied correctly.

Atlas/API v2 work was completed in a deliberately narrow support-contract form. Leo and Sarah’s internal examples now cover at-least-once webhook delivery and idempotency by event ID, cursor pagination versus fresh polling, and JWT clock-skew/JWKS checks. Each example is tied to logs and request IDs. There is no hidden reliability roadmap, product-priority change, staffing signal, or Jake review lane unless logs show a real product-priority or sequencing issue.

The webhook example says non-2xx deliveries may be retried and customers should dedupe by event ID or delivery ID before side effects. Morgan rejected any statement about exactly-once semantics, future enterprise connector behavior, or fixed retry timing because production retries use backoff and jitter. A safe support sentence explains that delivery is at least once and the same event may be delivered again, so handlers should commit safely and dedupe by event ID. Acme confirmed that deduping by `scaffold-delivery-id` fixed its QA handler. Leo’s PR `scaffold/atlas#224` removed the future exactly-once line and merged as ordinary support-contract clarification. The thread is closed with no customer decision, roadmap hint, data-loss concern, or founder escalation.

Cursor guidance says customers should use cursors during an active page sequence, persist a durable checkpoint, and resume from the last processed object if a cursor expires. A Growth customer asked whether to abandon cursors and run a full fresh poll every minute after receiving `cursor_expired_after_24h`. Request IDs `req_cur_8841` and `req_cur_8842` showed that the customer paused more than 24 hours and reused an expired cursor. There was no API defect or data-loss report. Support should recommend resuming from the durable checkpoint and ask for request IDs only if behavior continues after that. Fresh polling must not be described as the normal workaround.

JWT guidance remains fixed at five minutes of clock-skew leeway, with NTP/time synchronization and JWKS freshness checks before further investigation. A customer requested ten-minute tolerance; request IDs `req_jwt_7712` and `req_jwt_7713` showed the token was about seven minutes ahead, with valid `kid`, normal JWKS freshness, and no other expiry issue. The response should say to correct NTP or node clocks and send request IDs and token metadata if failures continue. A stale support-rotation sentence allowing ten-minute skew during enterprise migrations was removed on August 11. The stable guidance is now five-minute leeway, JWKS checks, and request IDs, with no customer-specific exception or Jake product-priority review.

Legal and procurement language remains cooperative but non-precedential. Morgan is comfortable confirming shipped SSO, documented connector behavior, ordinary support for platform defects, and normal account/product feedback capture. Morgan rejects customer-configurable retention/deletion controls, 24-hour removal obligations, a 90-day roadmap SLA for missing admin-event controls, custom connector workarounds, customer-specific identity/admin changes, or any commitment to absorb future identity or permission-model changes. Proposed security-addendum language should accept the shipped-support portions while redlining those commitments rather than sounding evasive.

Northstar Ventures remains warm but outside any process. After the July 13 casual coffee, Sofia received a request for a September catch-up if Q3 evidence became “more interesting,” followed by a generic Series C diligence checklist requesting a data-room index, customer proof points, and September availability. Morgan instructed Sofia not to schedule, hold a date, send materials, refresh the data room, or turn internal Compass/evidence work into investor-facing material. The CRM row is now `warm_later_after_july13_coffee_no_process`; the next touch is only after the September operating evidence read if Morgan independently decides there is something nameable to share. Notes and replacement tags explicitly record no process, no materials, no September hold, no data room, and no investor-facing Compass material. Sofia’s board-safe answer is that Mercury cleanup is support-quality hygiene, Atlas examples are internal and not finished as a reliability-roadmap item, Compass remains internal, and there is no financing narrative change.

Personal and household boundaries remain calm and private. Morgan and Jamie became privately engaged on March 19 in Oakland. After a July 27 logistics conversation, they agreed not to search for a 2026 venue or date, ask family to hold weekends, contact venues, pick dates, or turn the engagement into an open project. Any real planning begins with one private autumn logistics block after Jamie’s October schedule is known. Morgan’s mother was asked warmly not to hold the first weekend of November or any other family weekend. Close family and a few close friends may know; Maya received permission to tell Nora and Ali and show the ring photo quietly, but there should be no social posts, planning drift, or family logistics thread.

Kibo’s health remains stable within existing arthritis and stair-hesitation precautions. On July 25 his paw looked normal after two short walks and a rinse: no licking, swelling, bleeding, or abnormal movement. The walk stayed flat and short because Oakland was warm, and Morgan did not treat it as a vet issue. Later warm-weather guidance became stricter after Kibo panted and turned back during a late-morning walk, then ate normally without vomiting, leg favoring, or refusal of flat ground. On hot days he should walk before 10:30 AM; if that window is missed, skip the walk rather than making it up at midday. If stiff, walks remain short and flat. A walker’s 11:45 AM opening was declined for heat-timing reasons, not because of a concern about the walker. Kibo remains on strict no-poultry care; Morgan thanked Mom but declined plain chicken despite her concern about his stiffness. A building water shutoff was scheduled for Tuesday, August 11 from 9:00 AM to noon, with a calendar hold requested early enough to fill the kettle and Kibo’s water bowl.

Other household logistics included a Cactus Taqueria order for two grilled chicken burritos without sour cream, guacamole, chips and salsa, and an agua fresca, with salsa on the side. Maya requested birthday ideas for Mom in the $80–$120 range; Morgan noted Mom enjoyed last year’s ceramics class more than a physical gift and wanted only a few concise options rather than a long sibling planning thread.

Across the full period, Morgan’s recurring emotional and personality pattern is thoughtful but overloaded, terse, highly protective of boundaries, and relieved when work is closed. Morgan is not avoiding ambition; rather, they are determined not to let clean but ordinary evidence be inflated into fundraising, product, staffing, or customer promises. The live posture through August 13 is therefore: July close is standard Growth usage and vendor hygiene; Mercury is setup/support-quality work; Atlas is narrow support-contract clarity; Compass is internal-only; Evergreen remains on standard terms and included current-state/admin scope; hiring is closed; Northstar is warm-later with no process; legal avoids roadmap and customer-side-change commitments; Kibo’s care emphasizes heat timing and no poultry; and engagement/family matters stay happy, private, and non-operational.

messages.content: [2025-01-20T12:14:00-08:00] Can you make a compact Tuesday working-session agenda for Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo, and Sarah? For each Compass v0.1 signal I want the group to answer: what action should this trigger, who sees it, what evidence and caveat travel with it, what account note/source quality has to be true, and what we are explicitly not building. Keep the no-board-dashboard and no-new-hiring-lane boundary in the agenda.

[2025-01-22T09:18:00-08:00] Please create a doc titled “Compass v0.1 action-trigger checklist” from these notes. Make the body a compact owner checklist with signal, trigger, who sees it, evidence/caveat, source-quality requirement, and an explicit not-building line. Keep Anna, Nadia, Jake, Leo, and Sarah’s ownership clear, and keep the no-board-dashboard/no-new-hiring-lane boundary in it.

Compass working session - rough notes
Date: January 21, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Context for this session
- Goal was to get Compass v0.1 out of abstract "useful signals" territory and into: what should actually happen when a signal appears.
- Repeated boundary in the room: no board dashboard and no new hiring lane.
- Jake repeated that January Mercury activation is still the center of gravity, so Compass cannot quietly turn into a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.

Signals discussed

1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- Morgan: this only matters if it causes a named person to do something for a real account. If it just labels an account as risky, it becomes internal theater.
- Anna: definitions and caveats have to travel with the signal. "Renewal risk" by itself is too blunt and will be over-read.
- Nadia: useful only if it points to a named account-owner follow-up and the specific admin friction causing the risk.
- Sarah: account thread often mixes customer statement, support readout, and internal interpretation; if those are not separated, the signal will look more certain than it is.
- Working shape:
  - signal should identify the specific admin friction, setup-control issue, or role confusion causing the apparent risk
  - should point to the account-owner follow-up, not just surface a category
  - should not collapse true product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one bucket
- Open question: what is the minimum evidence package before Nadia will let this become an account-team script instead of an internal FYI?

2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- Nadia: wants a customer-growth/account-team script, not another metrics view.
- Jake: trigger cannot fire too early. It should happen only after first live sync is actually live and the teammate-invite/admin-role basics are visible.
- Morgan: this should be about timely next action after first real traction, not generic upsell language.
- Leo: before anything leaves the current team, he needs to check the data/platform seam and make sure the underlying event path is defendable.
- Working shape:
  - trigger only after first live sync is live
  - teammate-invite/admin-role basics need to be visible enough that the follow-up is grounded in actual account state

input.title: Compass v0.1 working-session agenda (reconstructed — Jan 21, 2025 session)
input.body:
Date: January 21, 2025
Participants: Morgan Chen, Anna Martinez, Nadia Singh, Jake, Leo Park, Sarah Kim

Purpose
Move Compass v0.1 out of abstract "useful signals" territory and into: what should actually happen when a signal appears.

Boundaries in the room (repeated at open and close)
- No board dashboard.
- No new hiring lane — stay inside the current lightweight staffing model.
- Do not let Compass turn into a prettier internal dashboard.
- January Mercury activation stays the center of gravity; Compass cannot quietly become a dashboard/platform build while that work is active.
- Keep the first pass narrow enough to actually test whether signals produce action.

For each signal, the group worked through: what action it should trigger, who sees it, what evidence/caveat travels with it, and what account-note/source quality has to be true.

1. Renewal-risk / admin-friction
- Morgan: only matters if it causes a named person to do something for a real account; otherwise it's internal theater.
- Anna: definitions and caveats must travel with the signal — "renewal risk" alone is too blunt and will be over-read.
- Nadia: useful only if it points to a named account-owner follow-up and the specific admin friction causing the risk.
- Sarah: account threads mix customer statement, support readout, and internal interpretation — if not separated, the signal will look more certain than it is.
- Working shape: identify the specific admin friction/setup-control issue/role confusion; point to the account-owner follow-up, not just a category; don't collapse product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one bucket.
- Open question: what is the minimum evidence package before Nadia will let this become an account-team script instead of an internal FYI?

2. Post-first-live-sync expansion prompt
- Nadia: wants a customer-growth/account-team script, not another metrics view.
- Jake: trigger cannot fire too early — only after first live sync is actually live and teammate-invite/admin-role basics are visible.
- Morgan: about timely next action after first real traction, not generic upsell language.
- Leo: needs to check the data/platform seam and confirm the underlying event path is defendable before anything leaves the current team.
- Working shape: trigger only after first live sync is live; teammate-invite/admin-role basics visible enough to ground the follow-up in actual account state; evidence should distinguish observed usage from inferred readiness for broader usage.
- Open question: what is the smallest useful post-first-live-sync prompt that changes behavior without becoming a new product surface?

3. Account-note source quality
- Sarah: source quality is uneven — some thread notes are reliable and traceable, some too thin to support follow-up.
- Anna: caveats need to travel here too; weak notes shouldn't masquerade as a clean signal.
- Nadia: doesn't want outreach based on mushy notes or internal inference dressed up as customer fact.
- Working shape: before a signal is used, Sarah should be able to say whether the underlying thread note is reliable, mixed, or too thin; provenance matters (customer statement vs. observed usage vs. support-derived fact vs. internal interpretation); if note quality is weak, the caveat should be explicit or the signal should stay internal.
- Open question: what note fields or source tags are required before this can feed a real follow-up?

Owner notes from discussion
- Anna Martinez: keep definitions and caveats attached to each signal so they don't get over-read.
- Nadia Singh: wants customer-growth/account-team scripts and follow-up logic, not a prettier metrics layer.
- Jake: v0.1 cannot become a dashboard/platform build while January Mercury activation is still active.
- Leo Park: needs a data/platform seam check before any signal is shown outside the current team.
- Sarah Kim: can separate reliable account-thread notes from notes that are too thin — source hygiene is a gating input, not cleanup.

Loose follow-ups captured, not resolved
- Define what action each signal should trigger.
- Define who sees each signal first, and who should not see it yet.
- Define the minimum evidence/caveat bundle.
- Define the source-quality bar for using a signal outside the current team.
- Define the explicit "not building" line for each v0.1 signal.

Session summary: Morgan Chen continues to apply strict evidence discipline across company operations, customer support, fundraising, hiring, legal, vendors, board communications, and personal life. The consistent preference is for smaller defensible claims over larger speculative ones, with operating facts kept separate from customer evidence, activation or expansion claims, financing narratives, product strategy, reliability roadmaps, staffing signals, and investor materials. Morgan favors bounded, reversible decisions and repeatedly corrects language that could turn routine hygiene into Series C momentum, B-round efficiency, enterprise readiness, activation lift, customer-facing Compass proof, or a reason to reopen hiring.

The company remains in the post-Q2 durability-read posture: “durability over motion,” with Q3 focused on retention, margin discipline, standard-term customer work, Mercury and Atlas owner lanes, and bounded internal Compass evidence. The June 24 read and subsequent July close did not create a market-warming process, data-room refresh, investor packet, fundraising narrative, hiring reopen, customer-facing Compass decision, or director action. The Head of Customer Growth backfill and second Mercury engineering requisition remain closed. Morgan continues to insist that this is an operating choice, not runway distress, reduced ambition, a broad hiring freeze, or avoidance of growth.

By late July and early August, Monday triage requests consistently prioritized practical sequencing rather than formal status notes. Morgan wanted work ordered across Devon’s vendor/finance hygiene, Anna’s evidence grid, HR’s stale contractor wording, Leo and Sarah’s Atlas support-contract examples, Mercury support-copy issues, Evergreen customer follow-ups, Sofia’s Northstar relationship handling, Kibo’s care, and private engagement logistics. The standing boundaries were no staffing reopen, fundraising or market-warming process, prepaid-capacity or committed-spend story, Q3 expansion motion, customer-facing Compass claim, or wedding-planning thread.

July vendor and finance reporting stayed factual and ordinary. After a staging log-retention rollback, AWS projections moved around $19.7k on July 27, $19.5k on July 29, and approximately $19.6k at preliminary July close; Pinecone remained around $4.1k–$4.2k with no replay spike. The correct description is that AWS returned to normal monthly hygiene after staging cleanup and Pinecone remained normal monthly usage. Morgan rejected Devon’s draft language about “optional financing efficiency,” “fall financing optionality,” “B-round efficiency signal,” or “efficiency proof.” No vendor-risk trigger, prepaid-capacity need, financing-efficiency evidence, or change to the Q2 vendor-hygiene posture exists.

AWS offered an estimated 7% savings for a 12-month, $240,000 compute commitment by August 21. Morgan declined both the committed-spend path and a subsequent no-commitment executive savings briefing, explaining that normal monthly usage does not make either useful. AWS accepted the decision and the only revisit condition is after August close, and only if sustained baseline usage materially changes. This is closed as a vendor-hygiene item, not a financing or vendor-risk thread.

The final July close showed Evergreen Bank at 228 monthly active developers, one standard Growth overage band under existing annual Mercury Growth terms. AWS closed around $19.5k and Pinecone around $4.1k, with no replay spike. There was no contract change, prepaid-capacity need, vendor-risk issue, department carveout, overage cap, custom admin package, or commercial exception. Morgan directed Anna’s `Q3_2026_Operating_Evidence_Working` deck, slide “July bounded operating evidence,” to describe July only as standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene—not market-warming, an expansion package, expansion pressure, financing proof, or a headcount trigger. Sarah’s customer note to Evergreen was intended to be clear and boring: 228 MAD is one standard Growth overage band, not a package adjustment, and existing standard terms remain in place.

Evergreen procurement asked whether 228 MAD implied a Q4 package adjustment or overage-cap discussion. Sarah’s bounded response should state that it does not: there is no overage cap, department carveout, custom admin package, or commercial exception; quarterly current-state/admin reviews remain included; and granular sync-operator interest is logged only as later advanced-admin input. Evergreen’s Q3 current-state/admin review remains within included scope. Granular sync-operator interest is not expansion evidence, a Compass repeatability signal, or a new commercial motion.

Anna’s Q3 evidence work was repeatedly narrowed. Her revised grid states that Mercury supported-source documentation and support macros are the stable source-caveat home while the empty state remains generic documentation discovery; Evergreen’s current-state/admin review closed inside included scope; and Atlas support-contract clarity continues through normal owner lanes. Morgan approved sharing the grid with Sarah, Leo, and Devon as internal evidence-hygiene context only, prohibiting labels such as board proof, Compass repeatability, activation lift, enterprise readiness, expansion evidence, or staffing signal. Anna later rewrote two overclaiming rows: July close should mean standard usage and monthly vendor hygiene, not expansion pressure or fall market-warming; and Atlas/Mercury work should mean owner-lane support clarity and setup-copy hygiene, not customer-facing Compass evidence or repeatability proof.

Anna also updated the bounded internal slide with exactly these themes: Mercury supported-source docs/support macros are the stable source-caveat home and the empty state is not activation or enterprise-readiness proof; Evergreen’s review closed within included scope and advanced-admin interest is not expansion or Compass repeatability; and Atlas examples are internal owner-lane clarity, not roadmap, reliability-roadmap, or customer-facing product proof. A Friday Q3 owner-lane read was designed around three narrow questions: support-quality improvement versus activation lift; Atlas support-contract clarity versus reliability-roadmap claims; and internal Compass evidence versus customer-facing repeatability. Sarah was to bring source-specific ticket counts, Leo whether the examples resolve webhook, cursor, and JWT questions, and Anna the current Compass owner-action rows. The read was explicitly not to become a broad evidence meeting about staffing, board messaging, or external proof.

Mercury remains confined to setup and support-quality work. The contractor-assisted source-picker documentation/support QA completed on July 23. HR’s old language—“Mercury contractor QA window open through August 7; monitor for follow-on need”—was declared stale. Morgan updated `mercury_engineering_headcount_plan` without changing `revisit_after` or `next_two_hires`; rationale tags now include `second_hire_on_hold`, `external_launch_readiness_feedback`, `no_arbitrary_month_end_revisit`, `profile_depends_on_signal`, and `contractor_docs_support_qa_completed_no_headcount_change`. The plan note says the July 23 docs/support-macro QA completed with no full-time Mercury engineering path, headcount exception, or July hiring reopen.

HR later forwarded two senior engineering referrals touching Mercury setup and Atlas platform seams. Morgan wanted a polite response declining intro calls and any active process while leaving the profiles warm for a later evidence-based revisit. There is no second Mercury requisition, July hiring reopen, Head of Customer Growth backfill, or reason to create interview momentum from completed contractor QA. HR’s replacement ops wording should say the Mercury docs/support QA is complete and did not create a headcount decision, contractor extension, or July hiring-reopen signal.

Mercury customer issues continued to be classified as setup clarity rather than defects or product strategy. A Growth customer invited a teammate before connecting a first source; the teammate saw a blank workspace and assumed permissions were broken. Logs showed a valid invite, no authentication or delivery issue, and no sync problem. The customer reply should explain that the blank state is expected before the first source exists and that the next step is connecting a supported source. Priya’s UI adjustment was approved as a small copy change: use “Workspace admin” with helper text, “Admins can invite teammates and manage sources once the first source is connected.” This is setup clarity, not a permissions-roadmap item.

Priya’s proposed Mercury banner language—“prove your workspace is enterprise-ready” and “increase activation”—was rejected. The neutral direction remains generic setup language without activation, enterprise-readiness, or roadmap implications. A separate customer received a “Your workspace is live” email after source authentication succeeded but before the first data run completed. The first sync finished thirteen minutes later with no data loss or failure. Support should say the source connection succeeded, the first sync was queued and then completed, and no action is needed. Priya’s copy direction is to say “source connected” rather than “workspace is live” when records are not yet visible.

A short Mercury queue delay affected six workspaces on August 4: approximately 22 minutes due to lag in a background-worker autoscaling step. The queue drained by 8:30 AM, all syncs completed, and there was no data loss or recurring pattern. Customer support should transparently state that a temporary processing delay occurred, completed, and requires no action, without calling it a formal incident, enterprise-readiness issue, activation proof, or roadmap item. One affected customer later requested a formal incident or RCA for its compliance file. Jake and Sarah were to provide a factual note with the timing, cause, completion, mitigation, and no-action-needed language, while avoiding over-labeling it as a formal incident.

A separate Mercury issue involved a stale “member” label after a Growth admin imported two teammates by CSV and assigned workspace-admin roles. The label persisted for approximately ninety seconds until refresh, but logs confirmed the roles were correctly applied, invitations were sent, and there was no permission failure or source-sync issue. Morgan’s requested classification is a small setup/support-quality issue, not an advanced-admin roadmap matter. The customer response should acknowledge the stale label while confirming that the roles were applied correctly.

Atlas/API v2 work was completed in a deliberately narrow support-contract form. Leo and Sarah’s internal examples now cover at-least-once webhook delivery and idempotency by event ID, cursor pagination versus fresh polling, and JWT clock-skew/JWKS checks. Each example is tied to logs and request IDs.
